Sports.title: Fifa launches new attack on media over alleged ‘concerted effort’ to undermine Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
Fifa has issued a new statement alleging there is a “concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president” as pressure increases on Gianni Infantino.

The governing body issued the statement in response to Uefa confirming on Saturday that a “departure payment” was made to a female employee who is alleged to have been in a relationship with Infantino while he was the organisation’s general secretary – allegations Fifa dismissed as “categorically untrue”.

The Daily Telegraph reported on Friday night that the woman received a six-figure sum following the alleged relationship with Infantino. In a statement, Uefa confirmed a payment was made along with covering the fees for an MBA course, which it said was “in line” with regulations at the time.

Fifa told the Telegraph that “any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory”, and late on Saturday issued a new, broader statement attacking Infantino’s critics.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa’s member associations and continues to serve with their mandate. It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president.

“Those who do not have the support of Fifa’s member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa’s established democratic processes. Recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning Fifa and its president. Speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact, and repetition does not make an allegation true.”

Defending Infantino as a leader who has “dedicated more than 30 years of his professional life to European and world football”, the statement added: “Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress.

“Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, Fifa will challenge it directly and vigorously. Fifa’s responsibility is to its 211 member associations and to football around the world. We will not be distracted or diverted from strengthening the organisation, delivering for our member associations and continuing the work of making football truly global.”

Pressure has continued to mount on Infantino after the exposure and collapse of his plan to seek private investment in a company which would run Fifa’s competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cups. Fifa has said it will not accept any challenge to Infantino’s position before the election next March.

Uefa’s threat that its 55 member countries could boycott Fifa competitions remains in place, with the European confederation saying on Thursday that the withdrawal of the scheme “changes nothing”.

Sports.title: ‘It’s a true art form’: Nigeria goalkeeper Maduka Okoye on high fashion and life at Udinese
Sports.content:
When Maduka Okoye visited Paris fashion week for the Jean Paul Gaultier show, taking his seat in the front row alongside rapper Cardi B, the online reaction was swift. Within hours, footage of the Udinese and Nigeria goalkeeper was all over TikTok and Instagram – where his audience now stretches near to two million followers – transforming the appearance into a viral cultural moment that crossed beyond the boundaries of football.

Yet ask Okoye to reflect on his sudden explosion into the fashion ecosystem, and he frames it not as a pursuit of celebrity or status, but as a genuine interest in art. “Being at the Paris fashion week was really impressive,” Okoye tells the Guardian. “It was my first time really coming into contact with high fashion, and it was fascinating. It’s a true art form. I enjoyed it immensely, and since that moment I’ve become a much bigger fan of fashion than I was before.”

In an era where elite footballers are expected to be multi-dimensional figures – balancing pitch performance, personal branding, digital presence and commercial partnerships – Okoye embodies a generation navigating this global landscape with ease.

Crucially, he knows exactly where to steer the ship.

While some athletes run the danger of losing their bearings when the off-pitch spotlight intensifies, the goalkeeper draws a sharp, impenetrable line between his two realms.

“What happens off the pitch is one thing, what happens on the pitch is another,” he says. “You have to separate the two. I never let these two worlds collide. Even though marketing and personal branding are part of the business today, at the end of the day I am a goalkeeper, and my main job is to protect my team’s goal. Outside football, I pursue things that matter to me but my priority and my work remain between the posts. These two worlds don’t overlap. What I do off the pitch has zero impact on what I do on it, and those two spheres will never cross.”

Reinforcing that boundary is the daily environment in which Okoye operates. Playing for Udinese, nestled in the calm, industrious region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia, creates a vivid contrast with the flashing cameras of Paris or the hyper-fast churn of social media trends. For Okoye, who grew up in Düsseldorf, Udine offers an essential sanctuary.

View image in fullscreen Maduka Okoye arrived at Udinese after spells at Sparta Rotterdam and Watford. Photograph: Foto Petrussi/Udinese FC

“I grew up in a big city, so in my heart I am and always will be a city boy, used to the metropolitan rhythm,” he smiles. “However, as you grow older, you learn to appreciate the peaceful side of life. I really like Udine. It’s a human, quiet city. You have your peace there and you can focus 100% on your work. I’m genuinely happy to live here. The serenity in Udine is good for you as a person and makes you feel very comfortable.”

That quiet focus away from the noise is paying dividends on the pitch. Having arrived after spells with Sparta Rotterdam and Watford – where he only made two senior appearances – he has established himself as a cornerstone between the posts for Udinese. In a footballing landscape often obsessed with highlight-reel saves, Okoye is staying focused.

“I believe there is always room for improvement in every direction,” he says. “I’m very happy working here with a great goalkeeping staff. I’m on a good path, learning every day, and I can’t wait to show it on the pitch during the season.”

When asked which goalkeeper impressed him most during the recent World Cup, Okoye says: “I found Spain’s Unai Simón very impressive, especially towards the final stages. Not so much for making hundreds of saves, but for the way he remained inside the game, defending deep balls against France. For me, that was goalkeeping of the highest level.

“As I said, it’s not just about spectacular saves; it’s about managing those details. Overall it was a great World Cup, and for us young goalkeepers it was a fantastic learning opportunity.”

Okoye’s drive to absorb lessons from top-tier athletes extends beyond football. During a recent visit to the British Grand Prix at Silverstone, he met rising Italian Formula One driver Kimi Antonelli, taking the opportunity to study the mechanics of another high-level sport.

“It was fantastic. The whole Formula One experience was extraordinary,” Okoye says. “I think there’s so much an athlete can learn from other sports. Meeting the drivers, especially Kimi, was great. From the outside you only see the race on TV, but behind it there’s an immense amount of work going on. It was impressive to see how much effort and preparation go into competing at that level.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Maduka Okoye enjoyed his visit to the British Grand Prix where he presented Kimi Antonelli with his pole position award after qualifying. Photograph: David Davies/PA

Udinese enter the Serie A season with stability and ambition and, in Friuli, that means looking towards Europe. “Everything is possible,” Okoye says. “But I think we should talk about that again in February or March. First we have to get the basics right and take it game by game. Then we’ll see where we are. We certainly have the quality, the players, an excellent staff, and a solid club behind us. Udinese is a club where a player can really grow and make that leap in quality.

“For me, Serie A remains one of the best leagues in the world and I’m grateful to be part of it. The higher the level of the league, the happier and prouder I am to play in it. We’re working hard and can’t wait to compete against the best.”

There is also unfinished business with Nigeria. Watching the World Cup from his living room was far from ideal. “Obviously it would have been better to be part of it, but unfortunately we didn’t qualify,” Okoye acknowledges. “We’ll try again for the next World Cup. I still enjoyed watching it from the outside; I supported Germany, hoping they’d go a bit further. Now we look to the future, and I really hope to be there at the next edition.”

As football continues to evolve into a convergence of sport, entertainment and global culture, figures such as Okoye offer a compelling blueprint for the modern athlete. He is a player capable of sitting in the front row in Paris on Monday, studying a rival on screen on Wednesday, and commanding his penalty box on Sunday – all without losing his sporting identity.

“On a personal level, it hasn’t changed me at all. I’m still the exact same person,” Okoye says. “Of course, when it comes to business and my personal image, a lot of things have changed. Fortunately, I have a great team around me and we try to make the most of these opportunities. But I repeat: who I am hasn’t changed. It’s simply part of my professional journey.”

And what advice would Okoye offer a young footballer dreaming of putting on the gloves and following in his footsteps? The Udinese goalkeeper does not hesitate: “To work hard, believe in yourself, and have faith.”

Sports.title: How Trabzonspor shocked Turkish rivals to make Mohamed Salah their Black Sea saviour
Sports.content:
It began with a text sent during the World Cup. Ertugrul Dogan, the president of Trabzonspor, was watching Egypt when he picked up his phone and messaged his manager, Fatih Tekke. “Coach,” it read. “Do you want Mohamed Salah?”

Tekke’s response was immediate enthusiasm, though Trabzonspor’s initial push for Salah went under the radar. For weeks, Besiktas looked most likely to land the former Liverpool striker. In Turkish football, Istanbul’s Big Three – Galatasaray, Fenerbahce and Besiktas – have long held a financial and cultural monopoly on the Süper Lig’s marquee signings.

Istanbul is not the capital, but it is the undisputed financial, cultural and commercial heartbeat of the country and wider region. It came as a shock, then, when Salah opted for Trabzonspor.

The club are by no means minnows. They form part of the traditional Big Four alongside their Istanbul rivals. Yet the football-crazy port city on the eastern Black Sea coast lacks the cosmopolitan lifestyle Istanbul offers. What it possesses instead is devotion. Most Turkish cities lack a strong local football identity, with residents supporting one of the major Istanbul sides from afar. Trabzon is one of the few exceptions. The entire region eats, sleeps and breathes for its team.

Trabzon is like the Newcastle of Turkey: a proud, working-class city in the north-east with an industrial maritime past, deeply tied to its football club and trying to forge a new identity to adapt to the modern world.

Salah’s arrival has thrust a city that often feels politically and geographically sidelined into the global spotlight. This transfer is bigger than football. Trabzon wants to revitalise the city as a maritime trade, tourism and logistics hub. The arrival of the Egyptian superstar ensures an even bigger spotlight on the city.

View image in fullscreen An excited Trabzonspor fan decked in traditional claret and sky blue colours sports sunglasses decorated with new signing Mohamed Salah. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters

The chaotic scenes at Trabzon airport on Wednesday – when supporters turned the terminal into a sea of red flares, followed by tens of thousands packing Papara Park for his signing ceremony – demonstrated their fervour.

Salah could easily have accepted lucrative proposals in the Saudi Pro League or Major League Soccer, but their fan culture pales by comparison. Crucially, the 34-year-old remains in a highly competitive league in the Uefa zone; Trabzonspor need only navigate the playoff rounds for a place in the Europa League main stage.

“I am seeing a reception like this for the first time in my life,” Salah told the roaring crowd during his signing ceremony. “I came here to win trophies. I am here to bring titles to this club.”

Trabzonspor have played the role of disruptors in Turkish football – the Black Sea rebels who broke Istanbul’s stranglehold in the 1970s and most recently won the league title in 2021–22. Never before, however, has a player of this magnitude rejected Istanbul for Trabzon.

View image in fullscreen Salah takes a photo as the fans offer a hearty welcome. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters

The Turkish top flight is experiencing a renaissance. Leandro Trossard joined Besiktas after a title-winning campaign with Arsenal; Victor Osimhen continues to spearhead Galatasaray’s attack; while Nathan Aké and Mason Greenwood now line up for Fenerbahce. The league is also developing world-class homegrown talent, with Arda Güler at Real Madrid and Ferdi Kadıoglu at Brighton serving as prime examples.

Trabzonspor’s pursuit of Salah was executed in the shadows. The club deployed their former winger Mahmoud Hassan – known as Trézéguet – as their secret operative. Salah’s international teammate spoke with the Egyptian captain daily, to help convince him to consider the move.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There was a cultural element, too: moving to a welcoming, Muslim-majority nation where Salah and his family could feel immediately at home. Trabzonspor locked him into a two-year contract through to June 2028 and disclosed the financial details on the Public Disclosure Platform (KAP). Salah will earn a base annual salary of €10m (£8.5m) alongside a guaranteed €7m annual signing bonus, netting him €17m per season (€34m net over two years).

Because wages in Turkey are paid net, with the club covering all tax liabilities, Salah in effect takes home 50% more than his final Liverpool contract. The deal also includes performance add-ons, a 5% agent’s fee on gross wages and an extraordinary image-rights agreement granting Salah a 20% royalty on all personal merchandise sold through the club’s official TS Club retail network.

The commercial return was immediate. Within 24 hours of Salah landing, Trabzonspor sold more than 17,000 season tickets, generating £11m. President Dogan confirmed that total projected revenue from tickets, sponsorships and merchandise during the Salah era is expected to approach £22m, in effect self-funding the transfer.

View image in fullscreen Trabzonspor supporters unveil a banner celebrating Salah. Photograph: Nurgul Gunaydin/AFP/Getty Images

Crucially, Trabzonspor did not overextend themselves. Balanced by roughly €95m raised in player sales since last season, the transfer is manageable financially. Salah joins a side on an upward trajectory under Tekke. Languishing in 13th when Tekke took over in March 2025, the team recovered to finish eight points behind the champions, Galatasaray, in third and won the Turkish Cup.

Tekke added the Valencia defender Cenk Özkaçar and the Manchester United loanee André Onana in goal and Trabzonspor are in talks with Darwin Núñez.

Taking his favoured No 10 shirt, Salah steps into a side in the ascendant. Yet the challenge remains steep. Galatasaray have won four consecutive league titles, while Besiktas and Fenerbahce have spent lavishly this summer. Trabzonspor will be hoping his arrival serves as a catalyst for a change in fortunes.

For Trabzon and the eastern region, however, Salah’s arrival is far more than a transfer story. The tide could be turning back in the favour of the Black Sea Storm.

Sports.title: Premier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobs
Sports.content:
Nine of the 20 Premier League clubs will begin the 2026-27 season with a different man in the dugout than the one who ended the last campaign. Opta recently revealed that the only other seasons which started with so many men making their managerial debut for top flight clubs were 1888-89 and 1946-47; the inaugural season of league football and the first following the second world war. Neither occurred under normal circumstances yet the level of turnover this summer does not feel unusual. Job security has never meant less in the Premier League.

Adding in the recently appointed pair of Roberto De Zerbi and Michael Carrick – confirmed in March and May respectively – means this season will start with 11 teams led by coaches with less than a year in their hotseat. The median tenure of Premier League managers at the start of each season has never been so low.

The most recent similar season was 2016-17. Heading into that campaign, 10 clubs had managers with under one year in the role. But with respect to the current Premier League crop, the relatively new head coaches that summer included Antonio Conte, Pep Guardiola, Jürgen Klopp and José Mourinho. All had either already won the Premier League or would go on to do so.

With Arsène Wenger still at Arsenal, four of those considered the five big beasts of Premier League management were competing, with the other (Alex Ferguson) having retired three years earlier. By contrast, Mikel Arteta is the only man who has won the English league who will be starting 2026-27 with the chance to do so again. There was also only one such manager two years ago, albeit it was Guardiola with his bulging trophy cabinet.

As Arteta has a single championship win, this season begins with the fewest English league titles on the division’s collective CV in the Premier League era. The previous lowest at the beginning of a campaign was three in 1995-96 (thanks to Ferguson having two and Howard Wilkinson one) and 2019-20 (Guardiola two, Manuel Pellegrini one).

This is a natural byproduct of managers being younger and less experienced. The median age of Premier League managers is 46.9 years old. It was the same heading into 2024-25 but was last younger 20 years ago. The drop in age has not led to further opportunities for Englishmen.

Eddie Howe’s departure from Newcastle means there will be three English managers when 2026-27 gets under way. The total was the same at the start of the last two campaigns, though interestingly it will be a different trio this year (Carrick, Frank Lampard and Gary O’Neil) than 12 months ago (Howe, Scott Parker and Graham Potter). The standing of the six clubs led by these men is worth considering. Two of the current coaches are at teams that have just been promoted, while two from last season’s group were with sides that went on to be relegated. Opportunities with even relatively secure Premier League clubs are now rare for English managers, never mind at those with realistic title ambitions.

The top end of the division is likely to have a Spanish feel. The Basque region of Gipuzkoa is providing more head coaches to England’s top division than England, with Arsenal, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Liverpool led by men from that relatively small area of Spain. It’s plausible none of them will win the league given the presence of Manchester City (who themselves are under new management after a decade of Guardiola) but Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola are in charge of three of the leading four clubs in the title betting market, with Unai Emery’s Villa seventh.

Managers from overseas lessening opportunities for English coaches in the Premier League is simply following the trend on the pitch. Just 8.6% of available minutes went to players from outside Britain or Ireland in 1992-93 yet a new high of 69.6% was reached last season. It is a truly global competition at every level, including ownership and sporting directors.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The influence of the latter on recruitment decisions has blurred the line between being a head coach and a manager. Liam Rosenior said he was “extremely humbled and honoured to be appointed head coach of Chelsea Football Club” when he was appointed by the Blues in January. “It fills me with immense pride to become manager of this great club,” was Xabi Alonso’s line when he secured essentially the same gig less than six months later. Based on the announcements clubs made to herald news of their appointments, the Premier League currently employs 14 head coaches and six managers.

Regardless of what the sign says on Alonso’s office door, he should reflect upon his new club giving him a four-year contract when they haven’t kept a manager for as long as two years since Conte left in 2018, or three years since Mourinho’s first spell in charge over a decade earlier.

Rosenior learned this the hard way. He signed a six-and-a-half year deal yet Chelsea previously employed both Rafael Benítez and Guus Hiddink on interim bases for longer than the young Englishman lasted at the club. Head coach or manager, call it what you will. The profession has never offered shorter-term employment, or felt less English, in the Premier League.

Sports.title: Mason Mount injury overshadows Manchester United’s draw with PSG
Sports.content:
Manchester United managed a creditable 1-1 draw with the European champions, Paris Saint-Germain, in a Gothenburg friendly on Saturday but the result was overshadowed by an injury to Mason Mount.

The England midfielder, who joined United from Chelsea in 2023, has been hampered by injury problems since arriving at Old Trafford and he lasted fewer than 20 minutes after starting against PSG.

Mount, 27, appeared to suffer a foot injury in Sweden and, after discussions with coaches on the touchline, left the field to be replaced by Tyler Fletcher. Mount has been restricted to 54 league appearances – many of them as a substitute – during his first three seasons with United.

His side were 1-0 down to PSG at the time of his injury, having gone behind in the second minute through an Ibrahim Mbaye goal even though the French giants were missing many of their star players.

But Bryan Mbeumo equalised in the 32nd minute when Amad Diallo played him in after winning the ball back.

There were more injury concerns for United early in the second half when their 40-year-old goalkeeper Tom Heaton suffered a right hamstring problem while rushing out to make a clearance.

Mbeumo might have doubled his tally but for the fine form of PSG’s Matvey Safonov but the goalkeeper left the pitch to jeers after escaping punishment for clattering into Joshua Zirkzee way outside his area – an incident that may well have led to him being punished in a competitive match.

There were late chances for Fletcher, Shea Lacey and the captain, Bruno Fernandes, who linked up well with new arrival Youri Tielemans in an encouraging sign for the United manager, Michael Carrick.

View image in fullscreen Mason Mount (back right) started the friendly in Gothenburg but had to be removed with an apparent injury. Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty Images

“I enjoyed it,” Carrick told MUTV, United’s in-house television station. “Good challenge. Slightly different with the way they play. We should’ve scored more goals.

“It’s good for the boys sometimes to have to problem-solve and find their own way and I thought we did that. That prepares them for the season as well. In that respect there were a lot of things that maybe people don’t always see that we were quite happy with. There were some good signs there.”

United have two more friendly fixtures, against bitter rivals Leeds in Dublin on Wednesday and AC Milan in Wroclaw three days later, before launching their Premier League campaign away to newly promoted Hull on 22 August.

Sports.title: West Ham sink Pompey in Carabao Cup as Sullivan ignores advice to stay away
Sports.content:
In an unseasonable black bomber jacket, with heavy duty company beside him, David Sullivan took his seat. Against the advice of the stadium’s operators, unbowed by serious allegations placed against his name and the weight of public opinion, West Ham’s major shareholder, the former co-chair, sat with arms crossed, always conspicuous by his presence.

By beating Portsmouth in relative comfort, West Ham, the club where Sullivan’s name is no longer above the door, had secured a heartening Carabao Cup passage to the second round. There, they will be reunited with their former Premier League peers. The serious Championship business begins next Sunday at Burnley. Whether Sullivan travels north for that remains to be seen. It cannot be ruled out.

“Neither me nor the players,” said Nuno Espírito Santo when asked about the effect of the uninvited guest’s presence. “We’ll focus on the pitch. The noise that comes from outside cannot distract at all; we’re going to find a lot of noise. We focus on the game, they do their job, they did it well.”

Before kick-off, the London Stadium big screen showed a “countdown to walkout”, referring to the players’ arrival rather than to fans deserting the scene in protest. This being West Ham in 2026, any confusion would be understandable. Taking previous mutinies into account, and despite a summer of intrigue and anger, there were surprisingly few audible or visible signs of insurrection as season 2026-27 began, and an extended 90 minutes was played out.

Even with Sullivan’s arrival expected, the gate to the directors’ car park did not stage a welcoming committee, the lanes around the London Stadium quiet. Protests there have been a regular sight, targeting Sullivan and his departed associate Karren Brady.

Even once Sullivan’s presence was confirmed there was nothing resembling the barracking of last season. Instead, the loudest boos of the first half came at a hydration break at its midway point, with an odd choice of 90s rave musical accompaniment. The legacy of a North American World Cup continues to darken.

View image in fullscreen David Sullivan takes his seat at the London Stadium just after kick-off. Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty Images

Perhaps still-searing temperatures and a dose of early optimism had doused the fires raging when the Hammers’ drop was confirmed in May. Time-served Irons know plenty about relegation; their club has dropped down each decade since the 1970s; West Ham heritage indeed.

The kick-off chorus of I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles drowned out the Pompey Chimes ringing out from 9,000 away fans. As is usual at the London Stadium, the visiting contingent decried their surroundings and the Faustian pact struck for West Ham’s tenancy.

Football has rarely been in focus during West Ham’s summer of tumult, boardroom battles after Sullivan’s defenestration. So what of football? Carabao Cup Saturday served as a decent dry run for their attempt at a promotion campaign. The new West Ham closely resembled the former West Ham, though shorn of the £151m worth of player sales that took in Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville and Freddie Potts. Joël Veltman, the sole summer signing so far, came on with three minutes left.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In midfield, Edson Álvarez, who spent last season on loan to Fenerbahce, lined up alongside Lewis Orford, a 20-year-old it is hoped can follow the path of Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick and Mark Noble, the latter a mentor, into becoming a first-team regular. His was a successful introduction into the first team.

“The energy of the young players is really really important for us,” said Nuno. “It’s up to us to develop the young academy players. That’s the vision for the future.”

The torpor of a first 30 minutes of little footballing consequence was broken by a Portsmouth goal, scored by Adrian Segecic, via a deflection off Maximilian Kilman, an expensive purchase far too regularly on the crime scene.

It took 10 minutes for West Ham to awaken before Mohamadou Kanté’s pirouetting feint laid up Taty Castellanos to equalise. Mere moments later, Jarrod Bowen, the club captain staying on to lead his club back up, a rare adult in the room last season, lashed in their second. “Jarrod shows us every day his commitment,” said Nuno.

The goals evidenced a quality that ought to guide the club back to the Premier League with some comfort, though nothing should be taken for granted. “If you give them a slight opening they’re going to take it,” said the Portsmouth manager, John Mousinho.

Sullivan kept any celebrations to himself and returned for a second half that began with Castellanos nodding in Bowen’s cross. An afternoon that might have descended into a familiar seething pit of rage and resentment now offered grounds for optimism. Though just beyond the hour, a chorus of “Stand up if you hate the board”.

If Sullivan is no longer a board member he was its undoubted target. He has turned many a deaf ear down the years and continues to do so.

Sports.title: Versatile Bruno Guimarães gives Mikel Arteta options to shuffle midfield pack | Ed Aarons
Sports.content:
If there was one of his many assets Newcastle supporters grew to love above all about Bruno Guimarães then it was best summed up by the man himself after being unveiled as Arsenal’s new £75m signing. “That’s a tough one,” said the Brazil midfielder when asked what fans in north London can expect from him. “I would say I can pass the ball, run a lot and play like a warrior. I’ll never give up.”

After more than four years on Tyneside and having seen Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali precede Eddie Howe’s departure, Guimarães – who was devastated after missing a penalty for the Seleção in their defeat against Norway in the last 16 of the World Cup – was determined to seize his opportunity.

While his emotional statement released by Newcastle as his move to Arsenal was confirmed on Saturday said they “did everything they could to keep me”, at the age of 28 he clearly felt it may never come again.

Andrea Berta’s pursuit of Vinícius Júnior came up short this week after the Brazil forward signed an improved six-year deal with Real Madrid. But at least Arsenal’s sporting director was finally able to bring in a player who was first courted by the club in the early days of Mikel Arteta’s reign, and who will add to the outstanding crop of central midfielders at his disposal.

Edu Gaspar, Berta’s predecessor, is understood to have first enquired about Guimarães when he was still at Athletico Paranaense in Brazil before he joined Lyon in the January 2020 transfer window – a few weeks after Arteta’s arrival at the Emirates.

They were also interested when Newcastle won the race to sign him in January 2022 for €40m, which came back to haunt Arsenal when he scored in a 2-0 win that went a long way to them missing out on Champions League qualification that season.

That first of nine appearances is the only time he scored against Arsenal, but Guimarães always impressed in a variety of roles whenever he came up against them, including in the Carabao Cup semi-final Newcastle won 4-0 on aggregate in 2025. He has covered more distance, won more duels and committed more fouls against Arsenal than any other side since making his Premier League debut.

It was no surprise that Declan Rice – the only player in the division to have covered more distance than Guimarães in that period and who enjoyed their fair share of battles – was one of the first to welcome him to Arsenal with a message that said “come here and please no more fights, now we’re friends”.

It is hard to argue with Guimarães that Arsenal have “one of the best midfields” in Europe because last season proved it. Yet having gone all the way to the Champions League final before spending the summer with England, after suffering with neural pain in his hamstring and lower back since December, Rice must be treated with the utmost care in the coming months. Guimarães can provide cover for him in a box-to-box role and gives Arteta options to rotate his other midfielders more frequently.

View image in fullscreen Bruno Guimarães will provide box-to-box cover for Declan Rice, rather than engage him in midfield combat. Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

He did not seem to trust Christian Nørgaard, who has joined Everton, to deputise for Martín Zubimendi in the Premier League last year, and that led to the Spain midfielder running out of steam in the spring.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It was telling that the teenager Myles Lewis-Skelly started in his preferred position at the base of midfield during the title run-in, and against Paris Saint-Germain in Budapest for the Champions League final, having begun the campaign as a left-back. Guimarães showed at Newcastle he is capable of playing in a deeper role as well and Arteta must decide how to balance his plethora of options in a crucial part of the pitch.

While he could not match Mikel Merino’s goalscoring exploits for Spain,Martin Ødegaard showed signs that he is back to his best during the World Cup after another disappointing season for Arsenal that was again interrupted by injury.

Having missed out on Morgan Rogers, the onus will be on the Norway captain, Guimarães and last summer’s big signing, Eberechi Eze, to provide some creativity to an attack that struggled to break down the low block at times last season.

Arsenal are still in the market for a defender to cover the absence of William Saliba for an extended period, while they would like to bring in another forward to add to the signing of Christos Tzolis. Atlético Madrid’s Julián Alvarez or Bradley Barcola of Paris Saint-Germain would fit the bill, although it remains to be seen if they will bring in a marquee player without offloading Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus – who has interest from Napoli. Even if they do depart, the presence of another familiar face in the Brazil centre-back Gabriel should also help Guimarães settle into his new home.

“Big Gabi was very excited,” he told Arsenal’s website. “Every time he sent me the message: ‘We’ll wait for you, when will you come?’ I’m so excited to join them, not only the Brazilians, we have an amazing squad here. I’m so excited to meet the other players, to start training. I just want to give my best.”

Sports.title: Carabao Cup: Millwall keeper saves four penalties, Preston prevail in Goodison home game
Sports.content:
Alex Neil felt Lukas Jensen deserved his moment of glory after the fit-again goalkeeper saved all four QPR penalties to take Millwall through to the second round of the Carabao Cup.

After a 1-1 draw, with a late Mark Sykes own goal bringing Rangers level after Luke Cundle’s opener, Millwall won 2-0 in a shootout which included six missed spot-kicks. Jensen, back after a long injury lay-off, kept out penalties from Ilias Chair, Harvey Vale, Koki Saito and Kwame Poku.

The Millwall manager said: “To save four penalties is really, really rare. And to put in the context behind that, Lukas has been missing for 15 months – he had a bad injury and then came back and had a setback. I think he would have been dreaming about that moment for 15 months – making four penalty saves and being the reason we’re through to the next round. And I’m absolutely delighted for him because he’s a great professional and a good lad, so fair play to him.”

View image in fullscreen Lukas Jensen saves from Harvey Vale during Millwall’s shootout victory. Photograph: Andrew Fosker/Shutterstock

Burnley prevailed 4-3 in a shootout to book their place in the second round after the Championship club had been held to a 1-1 draw by League One Notts County at Turf Moor. Veteran defender Kyle Walker held his nerve with the winning kick after Clarets goalkeeper Max Weiss had saved from Emile Acquah and Jacob Bedeau.

Russell Martin celebrated his first competitive game in charge of Leicester with a 1-0 victory over Northampton thanks to Caleb Okoli’s first-half goal. The former Southampton and Rangers manager has been tasked with leading Leicester’s recovery following relegation to League One and overcame a spirited showing from League Two opponents at the King Power Stadium.

Andre Brooks scored on his debut as Norwich cruised to a 4-1 victory over visitors MK Dons. The Canaries made a blistering start at Carrow Road, pouncing on some sloppy defending to grab an early two-goal advantage. Mohamed Touré was put clean through by Kenny McLean after the Dons had made a hash of their first attempt to play out from the back and blasted home with just 40 seconds on the clock.

The hosts then made it 2-0 after seven minutes as Touré picked out Anis Ben Slimane who calmly found the corner. Norwich effectively settled the issue on 43 minutes when Brooks’ shot found the net via a deflection off Ben Chrisene, who was credited with the goal. The Dons pulled one back on 56 minutes through Ryan Wintle, but Brooks made it four just before the hour.

Tony Mowbray wants to see more cutting edge from his Blackburn side after his return to the club began with a comeback 2-1 win at League One Burton. Substitutes Andri Gudjohnsen and Jayden Fevrier netted late goals to secure victory after Zac Scutt’s opener. “We got there in the end.” Mowbray said. “We said at half-time that we should have scored four or five goals. Not could have. Should have.”

View image in fullscreen Jayden Fevrier celebrates scoring Blackburn’s second at Burton. Photograph: Andrew Kearns/CameraSport/Getty Images

Delano Burgzorg scored the winning penalty in the shootout after Jusef Erabi equalised in stoppage time for 10-man Preston to knock out Huddersfield. The game took place at Goodison Park, the former Everton men’s ground, due to Preston’s Deepdale pitch not being ready. Daniel Iversen saved two penalties, after a thrilling end to normal time that ended 1-1 when Erabi cancelled out Radinio Balker’s strike. Preston played 69 minutes without Lewis Gibson who was shown a red card.

Sheffield Wednesday’s manager, Henrik Pedersen, praised his team’s performance after they beat Championship side Bolton 1-0. Substitute Jamal Lowe scored in the 70th minute. Bolton had Xavier Simons sent off in the 56th minute when he received a red card after clashing with Harry Gray.

Pedersen said: “I saw a lot of steps in the right direction for our aggressive pressing, for our quick transition, more players higher up when we won the ball, more forward mindset. We keep on going, and they keep on working as a group. It means everything in this situation where we are.”

View image in fullscreen Players confront each other before Bolton’s Xavier Simons is shown a red card. Photograph: Lee Parker/CameraSport/Getty Images

Arkell Jude-Boyd scored the decisive spot-kick as Shrewsbury beat Salford 4-3 on penalties after a 1-1 draw. Both goalkeepers starred in a remarkable shootout in which nine penalties were missed before Jude-Boyd fired into the top corner.

An unlucky own goal from Ollie Norburn and a late strike from Robert Bozenik gave Stoke a 2-0 win over Oldham, while Birmingham booked their place in round two with a narrow 1-0 win at Championship rivals Swansea. August Priske’s goal a minute before the break proved decisive at the Swansea.com Stadium, the big Danish striker steering the ball into the far corner after Carlos Vincente had sent a cross back across goal following a long free-kick into the box.

Fleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor, described the only goal in his side’s victory over Chesterfield as “Ched Evans in a nutshell”. New captain Evans struck 14 minutes in to seal the Cod Army’s place in the second round. Lawlor said: “He was brilliant. He sets standards at 37, while also challenging the young lads. We can use him as a reference point. That’s how you prepare for a game of football, whatever he does, replicate it.”

Reading beat League One new boys Bromley on penalties as they sunk five flawless spot-kicks to go through to the second round after a 1-1 draw. Goalkeeper Joel Pereira proved the match winner, saving Ethon Archer’s spot-kick to claim a 5-4 victory.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Derby crashed out after a 2-1 home defeat by Championship new boys Lincoln, who deserved their victory in the sunshine at Pride Park and could have won by a bigger margin. It took the Championship newcomers less than three minutes to go ahead when Ben House steered in a corner via a deflection off Matt Clarke. Lincoln extended their lead when a superb pass from Freddie Draper released Dom Jefferies to fire into the bottom right corner in the 23rd minute. Derby offered little until first-half stoppage time when Sam Szmodics struck from 25 yards.

View image in fullscreen Lincoln’s Ben House, centre, celebrates scoring their opener against Derby. Photograph: Chris Vaughan/Getty Images

The new Watford head coach, Alessio Dionisi, admitted he was relieved after his first game in charge needed a dramatic 99th-minute winner to sink League Two Crawley 1-0 at Vicarage Road. Dionisi, the Hornets’ 15th full-time appointment in seven years, watched his side squander a string of chances until Marc Bola’s 25-yard rocket.

The Italian said: “In the first half we played good, in the second only so-so. It is true we had a lot of shots and I agree it is better to win 1-0, but after 90 minutes it was 0-0 and to win football matches you have to score.”

Cambridge United mounted a speedy comeback to beat Barnet 2-1. The visitors went ahead soon after half-time, but the Us hit back through Ben Knight and Isaac Heath to lead only eight minutes later. Leyton Orient struck late to seal a 2-0 win over Oxford at Brisbane Road, with both goals coming from crosses by Charlie Wellens, the son of manager Richie, who only came on after 84 minutes. AFC Wimbledon scored a late equaliser before beating League Two Newport County 5-4 on penalties.

Luca Moore’s late header earned Crewe a 2-1 victory over Accrington. The tie appeared destined to end in spot-kicks, but there was late drama five minutes from the end of normal time when Moore pounced just as John Doolan’s side seemed to be gathering momentum. Doncaster advanced into the second round with a 5-4 penalty shootout win over Stockport after the game had finished 1-1 over 90 minutes. Rovers’ keeper Tommy Simkin proved the hero, keeping out efforts from Ben Osborn and Eoghan O’Connell.

Charlton progressed with a 3-1 win at League Two Cheltenham. Nathan Jones’ side opened up a three-goal lead before half-time, with Matty Godden, Sonny Carey and Tyreece Campbell on target.

Substitutes Cyle Larin and Romeo Akachukwu scored inside the last 18 minutes to give Southampton a 2-0 victory at Colchester, while West Brom coasted into the second round with a 4-1 win over Rotherham. The damage was done early on with goals coming from debutant Jimmy Jay-Morgan and Harry Whitwell to make it 2-0 at the break. Albion then doubled their lead in a dominant second half.

Barnsley beat Wigan on penalties after the tie had finished 1-1 in normal time. The first 10 spot-kicks were scored before Jon Mellish’s effort was saved by the knee of Rogan Ravenhill and Josh Earl scored to make it 6-5. Jack Moylan scored the winner on his Cardiff debut as the Championship new boys squeezed into the second round with a 3-2 win over League Two Swindon. Moylan – who joined Cardiff in midweek from Lincoln – curled in the winner in the 77th minute.

View image in fullscreen Cardiff’s Jack Moylan celebrates with Joel Colwill after scoring their third against Swindon. Photograph: Gareth Everett/Huw Evans/Shutterstock

League One Luton cruised to a comfortable 3-0 victory over League Two Gillingham. Goals from Nahki Wells, Benny Benagr and Gideon Kodua made sure Jack Wilshere’s side impressed at the Priestfield Stadium. Blackpool secured progression with a 3-1 victory over Grimsby at Blundell Park, while League One Bradford eased their way into the second round with a 2-0 win over Rochdale.

Harry Leonard ensured Bristol Rovers’ poor run in the Carabao Cup continued, his penalty securing Peterborough a 1-0 win at the Memorial Stadium. Leonard’s first-half spot-kick for the League One side meant Rovers have exited the competition at the first hurdle for seven consecutive seasons.

Sports.title: Anthony Elanga stretchered off in Newcastle friendly as horror challenge sparks touchline brawl
Sports.content:
Anthony Elanga stretchered off in Newcastle friendly as horror challenge sparks touchline brawl

Anthony Elanga was taken off on a stretcher on Saturday evening after being on the receiving end of a reckless challenge.

The Newcastle winger was clattered by Valencia's Jose Luis Gaya, with the tackle sparking a touchline brawl in Spain.

3 Elanga was stretchered off during Newcastle's pre-season clash with Valencia Credit: Getty

Elanga started in what was Matthias Jaissle's first game as Magpies manager following Eddie Howe's resignation.

But after 39 minutes and with his side 1-0 down, Jaissle saw one of his stars left writhing on the ground in pain.

Sweden international Elanga received the ball on the byline and neatly knocked the ball inside Valencia's Gaya.

However, the left back slid in, catching the Newcastle forward on the lower leg in what was a horror tackle.

Instantly, the Magpies bench cleared and some substitutes rushed toward the pitch, with players also sprinting over.

Jaissle made a studs-up movement to the linesmen, while four Newcastle players quickly squared up to Gaya.

A scuffle then broke out on the touchline, as both teams pushed and shoved, while Elanga remained lying on the grass.

Following some treatment, Elanga was eventually put on a stretcher and left the pitch with the medical team.

Thankfully, it has since been confirmed Elanga has not suffered a serious injury and is just struggling with a bruised shin.

And speaking post-match, Jaissle said he was 'in fear' for his player, adding: "It was tough. We're just happy it wasn't serious."

3 A pitchside brawl kicked off after Elanga was left grounded by Gaya Credit: Getty

3 Elanga received treatment as his teammates jumped to his defence in Spain Credit: Getty

Jacob Murphy took the place of his injured teammate, with Newcastle eventually turning the game around, going from 1-0 down at half time to win 2-1 thanks to two goals from Yoane Wissa.

Newcastle nightmare

As if Newcastle's summer hadn't been bad enough, their £55million winger was flattened just days before the season.

They kickstart their Premier League campaign on August 23 when they face Liverpool at St. James' Park.

The blow for Elanga comes hours after the Magpies sold their captain, Bruno Guimaraes, to Arsenal for £75m.

Guimaraes became the third star to leave the club this summer, following Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon out the door.

Toon also lost their manager in Howe, so recent months have been tough for the club, with Elanga's issue another problem.

So far, pre-season hasn't gone as planned either, drawing to Gateshead and losing 4-1 to Bristol City.

They do still have three friendlies to get ready for the top-flight campaign, with a clash against Everton next on August 12.

Newcastle also face Bayer Leverkusen and Strasbourg before the new season kicks off in two weeks' time.

Sports.title: Andy Carroll given straight red card for off-the-ball incident in non-league club’s season opener
Sports.content:
Andy Carroll given straight red card for off-the-ball incident in non-league club’s season opener

Andy Carroll kicked off Dagenham and Redbridge's National League South campaign with a straight red card on Saturday.

Carroll, who is assistant manager and a shareholder in the club, along with being a player, was sent off against Dorking Wanderers.

2 Carroll was shown a straight red card in Dagenham's 1-0 win over Dorking Credit: Getty

The ex-Liverpool, West Ham and Newcastle striker got himself involved in an off-the-ball clash that led to his marching orders.

The incident happened in the 56th minute of the season opener, with Carroll appearing to react angrily to being dragged down.

Dagenham's X account posted at the time: "Andy Carroll receives a straight red card for an off-the-ball incident."

Meanwhile, Dorking's post added more detail, as they wrote: "Carroll is sent off for a reckless challenge on Annesley. Louie is back on his feet after receiving treatment."

Tangle in the box

Footage was then shared on social media post-match by a fan who was watching the non-league game from the stands.

Carroll was shown being dragged down to the pitch as a cross was whipped into the box, and he appeared to react to the clash.

He got back up off the ground and stumbled over to Dorking's Louie Annesley, who had also fallen over in the tangle.

The 37-year-old seemed to touch the back of his opponent's head, sending him rolling around in pain on the floor.

Carroll then did the same, flopping to the grass in reaction.

Fortunately for him, after his red, Dagenham managed to hold on to their 1-0 lead and win their first game of the season.

'Andy's been manhandled'

Dagenham manager Lee Allinson defended Carroll when speaking after his side claimed victory over Dorking.

"If it's a sending off then great, no problem, but I'm not so sure, I need to look at it back," Allinson said.

"Andy reckons he's looked at it, there's no arms swung, nothing landed.

"But I think it's easy to come for Andy and look for what he does, but I think he's been manhandled for 55 minutes.

"Not one free-kick went against him as he's a big, strong centre-forward."

Carroll was playing his 13th game for Dagenham since signing for the non-league side in July of last year.

2 Carroll is a minority shareholder and assistant manager at the Daggers Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

The former Premier League striker has scored six goals and provided two assists for the club over the last year.

And as mentioned, he is also an assistant manager for the Daggers, holding a minority share in the club too.

He works alongside YouTube star KSI, who became co-owner of the team in March, joining their ownership group.

Just weeks after KSI's arrival, he actually appointed Carroll as interim boss before going on to bring in Allinson.

Now, Carroll plays as well as helps lead Dagenham, continuing his long playing career that began in 2006 at Newcastle.

Across spells with the Magpies, Liverpool and West Ham, he played 248 Premier League games, scoring 54 goals.

Sports.title: Sandro Tonali sparks mid-game scuffle during ‘heated’ Tottenham pre-season clash
Sports.content:
A frustrated Sandro Tonali sparked an angry scuffle during what was a not-so-friendly friendly between Tottenham and Getafe.

Tonali, who joined Spurs from Newcastle for £100m earlier this summer, was angered by a challenge from Mario Martin.



4 Tonali was not happy with a kick he received from Getafe's Martin

After the Italian midfielder pushed Martin over when winning back possession, the latter reacted with a late dig.

As the Getafe star looked to regain the ball, he left a leg in as Tonali passed the ball forward, catching his opponent.

And that left Tonali furious as he then pushed Martin back and lost focus on the game, having all eyes on his rival.



He chased him and grabbed Martin's shoulder to turn him around, pushing him again multiple times, with one of them to the neck.

That caused a melee in the centre of the pitch, as players from both teams swamped around the two players.



Ben Davies rushed over to defend Tonali, with Archie Gray, Jan Paul van Hecke and Andy Robertson all jumping in too.

Robertson also had a quick pushing match with a Getafe player before things eventually calmed down in the 'friendly'.



Tonali and Martin avoided a booking for the incident.

'If you get kicked, you're going to react'

Post-match, Tonali was defended for his reaction that sparked the scrap, as Getafe took things too far in pre-season.

Van Hecke admitted that things got a bit too aggressive in the friendly that was being played behind closed doors.

4 Tonali won the ball back but then got caught by a late challenge from his opponent

4 The Italian then ran after Martin and pushed him multiple times



“Sometimes it’s good [to have a physical game]," he admitted.

“I thought today was a bit too much. A bit from their side, sometimes it’s not necessary, especially in a friendly.

“I think in a normal game maybe they have two or three red cards.

"But that’s also maybe the way they play. We knew beforehand that they can do it.

“But then it’s a friendly, so sometimes you think maybe a bit less, but on the other side we also need to be at our top then because if you don’t put in your foot then they are going to win it.

“If that’s what the game asks, you also need to put your foot in and battle with them, otherwise they win the battles.



4 Spurs and Getafe players swarmed around Tonali and Martin as things got heated

"That’s what you don’t want, that’s the first thing in football you need to win.

“You saw sometimes it got a bit heated, but that’s because of the reaction, if you get kicked, then you’re going to react.”

Tottenham drew with Getafe in the feisty affair on Saturday as Conor Gallagher netted following Alberto Risco's opener.



They now only have one more pre-season game to play before the Premier League campaign kicks off on August 22.

Spurs take on Hoffenheim at 3pm on Saturday, August 15 next.
