World.title: Harvesting rainwater from rooftops could cut the number of heatwave days and reduce air con reliance
World.content:
Rooftop rainwater could be a secret weapon in tackling extreme heat, following Europe’s blistering summer.

 

New research from The University of Manchester in the UK modelled a system that stores rainwater harvested from rooftops and automatically sprays it onto buildings during hot weather.

The study, published in the science journal Earth’s Future, found that cooler roofs transferred less heat into buildings, lowering the demand for air conditioning and therefore cutting energy consumption usually needed for cooling.

Less air con also means less heat waste would be released into the city. Together, researchers say these effects could help reduce urban temperatures, cutting the number of heatwave days overall and lessening the intensity of extreme heat events.

Rooftops can act as ‘strategic cooling’ for cities

The study, which used the city of Tokyo as a case study, suggests that the time at which sprinklers were switched on – for example, when the roof reached a certain temperature – had a greater impact than either the size of the tank or the amount of water applied.

It also found that bigger is not always better. In fact, very large tanks delivered only “modest additional reductions” in energy use and extreme heat, while applying extra water did not always lead to more cooling because some of it remained on the roof instead of evaporating.

“Cities around the world are facing growing challenges from extreme heat,” says lead author Dr Zhonghua Zheng of The University of Manchester.

“Air conditioning can help keep people safe and comfortable but it also consumes large amounts of energy and releases additional heat into the urban environment. Our study shows that harvesting rainwater from roofs and using it strategically for cooling could provide a practical way to reduce both energy demand and urban temperatures.”

Dr Zheng adds that the benefits of harvesting rooftop rainwater become “even greater during hotter years”, suggesting that the approach could become increasingly important as the climate continues to warm.

The study could help local authorities and urban planners evaluate how rainwater-based cooling systems might work in their own regions, while considering practicalities such as cost and water availability.

“The rainwater tank also provides an additional co-benefit on reducing the extreme urban runoff,” says Junjie Yu, PhD researcher at The University of Manchester.

“This approach exemplifies a ‘natural solution to natural challenges’, in which rainwater serves as a natural resource to mitigate both thermal stress and hydrological extremes.”

Why air con isn’t the best way to tackle extreme heat

The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that space cooling – which is mostly air conditioning, but also includes fans – consumed around 2,100 terawatt-hours (TWh) of power in 2022. That’s around seven per cent of the world’s electricity from that year.

Experts warn that air con units could triple in the next three decades, reaching a staggering 5.5 billion installations, as extreme heat becomes the ‘new normal’.

It’s triggered concern that increased demand will put additional strain on Europe’s already struggling energy grid, and send emissions spiralling.

While air conditioning could theoretically be powered by clean energy such as solar power, concern remains over the use of refrigerants such as hydrofluorocarbon and hydrochlorofluorocarbon. These are powerful greenhouse gases that trap thousands of times more heat in the atmosphere compared to CO2.

The EU and UK are actively phasing out fluorinated gases in favour of natural refrigerants such as hydrocarbons (like propane) and CO2, which are far less damaging to the climate – but propane’s flammability makes installation complicated.

Still, the very process of absorbing heat from inside a home and dumping it outside contributes to the urban heat island effect. This is when heat is trapped between tall buildings and absorbed by the large amounts of asphalt and concrete found in cities before being released back into the air.

It is why larger cities tend to experience stronger heat stress and higher maximum temperatures than nearby rural areas.

How ‘cool roofs’ can also help tackle heatwaves

A 2024 study by UCL and The University of Exeter analysed the cooling effect that roofs painted white or other reflective colours (known as ‘cool roofs’) would have on London’s air temperature between June and August 2018.

At the time, this was one of the city’s hottest summers on record, with the average temperature during those three months hitting 19.2C – about 1.6C warmer than average for that time of year.

The paper found that had cool roofs been widely installed through London, the city could have cooled by about 0.8C on average.

“If widely adopted, cool roofs can significantly reduce the ground-level air temperature of a city,” says lead author Dr Charles Simpson from the UCL Bartlett School Environment, Energy & Resources.

“The resulting cooling effect across the city would save lives and improve the quality of life for residents throughout the urban area.”

World.title: Two drones spottled flying over military base in the western part of the country, German armed forces say
World.content:
Two drones were spotted flying over a German military base in the western part of the country, just two days after a drone carrying explosives was found at a key cargo airport, the German Armed Forces said in a statement on Saturday.

 

Security surveillance at the Bundeswehr base in Mechernich reported seeing two drones around 10 pm on Thursday, according to a statement from the German Joint Force Command. The sightings were confirmed and military police forces were deployed to the site.

The military said the Euskirchen police department has opened an investigation. The police did not immediately respond to a request for comment and the military did not release additional details.

Recently, drone sightings over civilian and cargo airports have been more widely reported.

'New quality of danger'

Last year, mysterious drone flights over the airspace of European Union member countries alarmed the public and authorities, and also prompted the cancellation of dozens of flights that stranded thousands of passengers at several major airports from Copenhagen to Warsaw.

Thursday's sighting of the two drones came after a drone with explosives was found at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle Airport shortly before midnight on Tuesday. The device and its detonator were destroyed in a controlled explosion, with German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt calling the incident a “new quality of danger.”

Leipzig-Halle is a major hub for international freight and for providing support to Ukraine. Since Russia’s war on Ukraine broke out in February 2022, it has also doubled as a base for Kyiv’s national cargo carrier, Antonov Airlines.

It is also home to NATO’s Strategic Airlift International Solution, or SALIS, which is currently operational almost every day in delivering equipment to NATO battle groups along its eastern flank from Finland to Romania and supporting EU and alliance nation missions.

In 2024, an incendiary device ignited at a logistics centre at the airport and set fire to a freight container, part of a plot that Western security officials suspect was organized by Russian intelligence.

Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.

The Russian Embassy in Germany on Friday called the Leipzig drone incident part of a “new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany.”

World.title: Wedding at Funchal cathedral, but not Cristiano and Georgina's, to the disappointment of hundreds
World.content:
At around three o'clock on Saturday afternoon, hundreds of people began to gather outside Funchal's Sé Cathedral in Madeira. The ceremony was running slightly late: the bride was missing, the last to arrive, as is customary.

 

Outside, around two thousand people with their mobile phones held aloft tried to capture the precious moment; many will have managed it, but when they realised that the bride was not Georgina Rodriguez but Nicole, and those who did get into the church saw that it was not Ronaldo standing by the altar but Fábio, they will surely have been left disappointed.

For this expat couple now living in France, it will have been a particularly lively ceremony. "We feel like celebrities," one of the guests joked to the Diário de Notícias da Madeira (source in Portuguese).

Some people travelled to Madeira especially to attend what would have been the most talked-about wedding of the year, if the rumour spread by the British tabloids had been confirmed.

That was the case for the eldest daughter of Helena Ferro Gouveia, a former journalist and commentator on CNN Portugal, who said her eldest, a "die-hard fan" of Cristiano, travelled specially from Germany to "catch a glimpse of the wedding" of Fábio and Nicole.

For now, however, the details of the nuptials remain nothing more than rumours fuelled by the national and international celebrity press. Imagination is not in short supply, with some outlets even providing details of an entirely fictitious ceremony.

Last week the press was adamant that Cris and Gio were going to get married at the Quinta da Regaleira in Sintra on Saturday, 2 August. This week, The Sun wrote that the ceremony would take place on 8 August at Funchal Cathedral, at 3 pm, and that the reception would be held at the Savoy Palace hotel, having discovered that on that very day the luxury hotel had reserved two floors for a private event.

The pressure from the international media has been so intense that the Funchal diocese decided to publish images of Saturday's wedding between Fábio and Nicole to help clear the churchyard.

"After a lot of confusion in the street with so many journalists and tourists, we finally managed to close the church and celebrate," the diocese wrote in a post shared on Facebook.

The rumours keep on gathering strength, especially on social media, where the famous couple has been betrothed time and time again. There are even AI-doctored photos and videos of the ceremony showing star guests such as Yamine Lamal, Mbappé, Messi and Neymar.

But it is also on social media that the rumours lose traction, particularly if you pay attention to the posts from the people closest to Cristiano.

Take his sister, Kátia Aveiro, for example, who this morning posted on Instagram saying that she was in Lisbon and would be staying in the Portuguese capital "for a few more days". Hard to imagine she would want to miss her brother's wedding.

World.title: Major wildfire in hills above Lake Garda: at least 200 residents and tourists evacuated
World.content:
A major wildfire broke out on Friday evening in Alto Garda, in the Tignale mountains on the western shore of Lake Garda. Firefighters, civil protection teams, forest Carabinieri and volunteer fire crews are on site working to secure the area. The response is being coordinated by the mayor of Tignale, Daniele Bonassi, who described the scenes as "terrifying".

 

The blaze has not yet been brought under control because of winds of up to 40 kilometres an hour, which are rapidly changing the direction of the flames. The area has been hit hard by the drought of recent weeks, leaving vegetation dry and highly vulnerable to fire. This morning two Canadair water-bombing aircraft were also deployed to try to stop the flames.

Wildfire in Tignale, firefighters in action Vigili del Fuoco

The authorities have ordered the evacuation of 200 people. Overnight, guests were moved out of holiday homes and the "La Forca" residence, which hosts many Italian and foreign tourists. Rescuers are going house to housebecause it is sometimes unclear which properties are currently occupied or used by tourists. So far, no injuries have been reported.

The cause of the blaze is still unclear, and for now rescue efforts are focused on containing the flames.

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: Indonesia: Mount Bromo wildfire grows, spurs park closure
World.content:
Indonesian authorities have closed a popular national park until further notice. Strong winds and rough terrain are making it difficult for firefighters to extinguish the blaze.

Authorities in Indonesia closed the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java until further notice on Saturday due to a wildfire that has scorched some 176 hectares (435 acres) of land on Mount Bromo since it began on Monday.

The blaze, one of several currently burning across Indonesia, has mobilized hundreds of firefighters, park rangers, police, soldiers and volunteers at one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations.

What do we know about the wildfires situation in Indonesia?

Helicopters and drones are in use in the air and firebreaks are being created by crews on the ground.

Officials describe the situation as challenging, pointing to high winds and rough terrain, with many areas difficult to access on steep volcanic slopes.

"These conditions make air operations important to reach areas that cannot be accessed optimally by land," one official said.

The blaze has mobilized hundreds of firefighters, park rangers, police, soldiers and volunteers at one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations Image: Muhammad Fajri/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Dry conditions and winds are fueling the spread of the flames according to Indonesia's Meteorological, Climatological and Geophysical Agency.

Authorities say the fire was sparked during land clearing work.

Though fires — often illegally started by plantation owners and farmers to clear for planting — are common in the region, the current El Nino weather pattern and seasonal dry winds from Australia have combined to make this year especially prone to wildfire and drought.

Indonesia has lost more than 107,000 hectares of land to fire in the first half of 2026, over twice the area destroyed in wildfires in 2023, when the last El-Nino pattern started.

World.title: India: Ex-Education Minister Pradhan says Gen Z 'misled'
World.content:
08/09/2026 August 9, 2026 Gen Z was 'misled,' says Dharmendra Pradhan

Former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan broke his silence for the first time since he resigned following massive youth protests.

Speaking at a ceremony on Saturday, Pradhan said: "Gen Z is our children. Some people attempted to mislead them."

Pradhan's acknowledgment of the protests and his resignation came some 15 days after he quit as the education minister.

Pradhan said he "suffered" because of Gen Z's stubbornness but had come to realize that the new generation must be understood rather than resisted.

Speaking about his resignation, Pradhan said he had approached Prime Minister Narendra Modi and offered to resign from the Union Council of Ministers.

"The post was not important to me," Pradhan told a gathering at an event at GM University in Bhubaneswar, according to Indian news agency Press Trust of India.

Pradhan's resignation was the biggest demand made by the young protesters, led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

The protests were triggered over exam irregularities in competitive exams, especially the NEET exam, which is a key requirement for those wishing to enter medical schools across India.

Reportedly, at least 21 students had taken their own lives after the NEET exam was cancelled because of a question paper leak. It was then held at a later date.

World.title: Australia: Jetstar, Qatar Airways planes almost collide on Sydney Airport tarmac
World.content:
A flight crew member was injured in a near-miss collision on the runway at Australia's Sydney Airport. An investigation has been launched to determine what caused the incident.

Two passenger aircraft — a Jetstar and a Qatar Airways plane — came close to crashing into each other on the tarmac at Australia's busiest Sydney Airport on Sunday.

A crew member was injured and the incident has triggered a probe by the country's safety regulators.

What do we know about the near-miss collision?

The Jetstar A320 was taxiing for takeoff to the Gold Coast in the state of Queensland when its flight crew saw the Qatar Airways Boeing 777 — which was being towed by an aircraft tug — in close proximity on a crossing taxiway, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said in a statement.

"Both aircraft were stopped abruptly", the statement said, leading to a Jestar cabin crew member moving through the cabin being injured and the connection between the 777 nose gear and aircraft tug suffering damage.

The injured crew member was treated by paramedics.

How are Australian authorities handling the incident?

The ATSB said that investigators were gathering data from both the planes, air traffic control, and interviewing crew and tug operators to determine the cause of the near collision.

The regulator put out a call for witnesses at the airport to send in any visuals of the incident.

Jetstar — which is a low-cost subsidiary of Australia's national carrier Qantas — said it was also conducting its own investigation.

"Our aircraft was following ⁠instructions ​by Air Traffic Control when the ​pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in ​close proximity," a ‌Jetstar spokesperson said.

There was no immediate statement from Qatar Airways, which is the flag carrier of Qatar.

Meanwhile, flights at Sydney Airport were experiencing delays following the incident, government agency Airservices Australia said.

Sunday's incident ⁠comes a day after Sydney Airport witnessed widespread delays ⁠sparked by Airservices Australia authorizing "departure spacing" due to roster issues with air traffic controllers.

08/09/2026 August 9, 2026 Germany's trade deficit with China grows in first half

New preliminary data released on Sunday has shown that German exports to China fell more than 12% year-on-year between January to June, while German imports from China rose 8.9%.

That raises last year's trade deficit of €40 billion ($46.2 billion) for the same period to some €55 billion.

The data from the state-run agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) reflects the decreasing reliance by Chinese firms on European imports.

They show that although China remains Germany's top trading partner, the Asian powerhouse is now only the ninth-biggest market for German goods, with far smaller economies like Austria and Switzerland buying more from Germany in 2026.

As recently as 2021, China was Germany's second-biggest ​export market.

The US remains Germany's single-biggest foreign market, despite a drop in German exports there amid protectionist tariffs introduced under President Donald Trump.

World.title: Canada: British Columbia declares emergency as fires spread
World.content:
More than 20,000 people have been forced from their homes by out-of-control wildfires in Canada's British Columbia, where 105 blazes are currently burning.

Canadian officials on Saturday declared a state of emergency in British Columbia after more than 20,000 people were ordered to flee a fast-moving wildfire.

Describing the intensity of the blaze, British Columbia Premier David Eby said a fire official compared it to "a bomb going off."

"He described flames on a 100-foot (30-meter) tree, flames going 200 feet above that, and the fire creating its own weather system, which creates lightning," Eby said.

"Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," he added.

Wildfire in British Columbia nearly doubles in size overnight

The fire, first reported Friday evening, grew rapidly overnight, triggering widespread evacuation orders.

By Saturday, it had spread to about 9,500 hectares (23,500 acres), prompting all 12,000 residents of the Summerland district to evacuate.

The Summerland blaze is one of many fires challenging emergency crews across British Columbia.

The province has seen 70 new wildfires over the past week, and 105 are currently burning, according to British Columbia Minister of Forests Ravi Parmar.

A dry and hot summer has ⁠led to more than ​4,500 fires in Canada this year [FILE: August 3, 2026] Image: Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

Canada grapples with large wildfires

Fires have scorched 4 million hectares in Canada in 2026, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Center .

Blazes flared up in several regions, including Ontario and Quebec, this year as hot, dry conditions fueled fires in dense forest areas.

In recent years, Canada has faced a growing number of destructive wildfire seasons.

World.title: FIFA warns against 'concerted effort' to undermine Gianni Infantino
World.content:
Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.

FIFA warned against what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

The statement, issued late on Saturday, comes amid a growing dispute over Infantino's leadership after the failed plan to create a subsidiary to run the men's World Cup and other events, with up to a 20% stake offered to external investors.

The proposal drew criticism from European governing body UEFA, which threatened to boycott future World Cups, as well as several national associations and senior FIFA officials, and prompted calls for Infantino to resign.

Amid the growing criticism Infantino persuaded FIFA's Board of Management to express its full support for him at a crisis meeting in Rabat, Morocco, on Wednesday.

FIFA accused of blackmail in exchange for Infantino support To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Report raises new questions over Infantino

The pressure on Infantino intensified on Friday when British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported a six-figure sum was paid to a female employee alleged to have been in a relationship with him during his time as UEFA general secretary.

UEFA confirmed a departure payment and said it also funded her MBA course, stating both were in line with regulations at the time.

A FIFA spokesman told the Telegraph on Friday: "FIFA president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue."

Responding to the latest scrutiny, FIFA said on Saturday, without directly mentioning the Telegraph report, "recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its President."

Investment plan dispute deepens leadership crisis

The fallout over the shelved private investment plan has overshadowed Infantino's bid for a fourth term as FIFA president.

After this week's crisis meeting, UEFA said it no longer has confidence in him, and Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness called for his resignation.

Despite the controversy, Infantino retains strong backing among FIFA members, with the Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously supporting his leadership and South American governing body CONMEBOL opposing any attempt to remove him without a vote of all member associations.

FIFA said that those who lacked the support of its member associations should not seek to achieve "allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA's established democratic processes."

World.title: Germany: Interior Minister warns of 'daily' hybrid warfare
World.content:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says attacks by foreign powers have become a constant threat to Germany. His remarks come just days after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt on Sunday warned that hybrid warfare attacks had become a daily threat to the country.

"We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag following the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

"Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality," Dobrindt said.

He also noted that the country is stepping up research into drones to address new security threats.

A new drone security research center will be established later in August at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, Dobrindt said.

Drone warfare: German startup draws on Ukraine's experience To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Drones spotted above military base in west Germany

On Saturday, Germany's armed forces confirmed that two drones had been spotted late on Thursday over a German military base in Mechernich in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia near the Belgian border.

The drones were detected at around 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) over the Bundeswehr base, a German armed forces spokesperson said.

German media reported that the base hosts personnel responsible for the maintenance of US Patriot air defense systems, which play a key role in defending Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks.

Drone incident at Leipzig airport

The sighting in Mechernich comes just two days after the discovery of a drone carrying explosives a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an incident Dobrindt called a "hybrid attack scenario."

While German government officials have refrained from publicly blaming any foreign country over the Leipzig incident, some lawmakers have pointed fingers at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since ​its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.

On Friday, the Russian Embassy in Berlin dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation" and said Russia was once more being accused of hostile actions "without the slightest evidence being presented."

World.title: Nigeria marries 1,500 couples in mass wedding
World.content:
The government describes the program as a way to support low-income families and promote social stability. Among those married were people who lost family members in violent attacks.

Some 1,500 couples got married at a mass wedding organized by Abba Kabir Yusuf, the governor of Kano state, in northern Nigeria.

The regional government described the two-day event as a way to support low-income families and promote social stability.

"The whole idea for the marriage is to help our families and we husbands who are not financially stable to marry; that's why the government is helping us get married," groom Abubakar Aliyu Musa told the Associated Press.

This is the second time Yusuf's administration has organized a mass wedding.

The two-day ceremony was held in northern Kano state Image: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

What else do we know about the program in Kano state?

According to Kano's regional government, each bride received a dowry of 200,000 naira ($147, €127) and support to set up a small business.

The couples were also given household items including beds, mattresses and blankets.

The couples underwent screening and counseling before the wedding.

Governor Yusuf described the program as a "bold social intervention aimed at restoring hope and supporting dignified family life in Kano."

"The program was designed not only to assist women who might otherwise struggle to afford marriage, but also to strengthen families and promote social stability in the state," he said.

Widower remarries in mass wedding

Among those who participated in the mass wedding were people who lost family members in violent attacks.

One of them was Haruna Bashir, who lost his wife and six children in an attack earlier in the year. Daurawa hailed the ceremony as a step toward Bashir "gradually returning to normal life" after having "hardly interacted with people … since the tragic incident."

Nigeria has been grappling with a major security crisis for years, particularly in the country's north, which is regularly hit by raids and attacks by Islamist insurgents and organized gangs.

Many armed groups in Nigeria also kidnap schoolchildren to demand large ransoms.

On Wednesday, the Nigerian government announced the release of 308 people who had been abducted.

World.title: Llega el día de las dos noches: millones de españoles buscan su lugar para ver el eclipse
World.content:
Con destinos del interior con lleno total desde hace más de un año y miles de personas que tomarán una decisión a última hora, España vivirá este 12 de agosto un fenómeno astronómico único que supondrá un desafío para las autoridades

El próximo miércoles 12 de agosto, pasadas las 20.25 de la tarde, cuando la Luna cubra por completo al Sol en el primer eclipse total en verse en la Península en más de cien años, el veterano astrónomo José Ángel Docobo les pedirá a las cientos de personas concentradas simultáneamente en el Altar del Sol, un monumento megalítico de Lalín (Pontevedra), y en la Playa de las Catedrales en Ribadeo (Lugo), que cuenten hasta tres y se quiten las gafas de protección para poder ver con sus propios ojos la corona solar. “Hay que mirar a ella, pero tampoco enamorarse, porque la totalidad en algunos lugares va a ser de segundos y hay que tener muchísima precaución porque enseguida va a volver la luz solar y no podemos estar mirando”, advierte.

Poder ver esa corona en directo —los filamentos plateados que rodean al sol— sin viajar a otra parte del mundo es algo extraordinario en la vida de una persona. Tanto que para Docobo, un catedrático emérito de 75 años que ha dedicado su carrera a mirar al cielo para estudiar las estrellas, será la primera vez. Y como le invitaron a narrar el fenómeno desde dos municipios gallegos separados por más de 200 kilómetros de distancia y no quería fallarle a ninguno, decidió hacerlo en los dos a la vez a través de una conexión satelital. Él estará en Lalín comentando en directo cada detalle de la jugada, como si se tratara de un “Jose María García astronómico”, bromea; y también le escucharán en el monumento natural de la Playa de las Catedrales a través de una pantalla gigante que colocará el ayuntamiento de Ribadeo, en la costa por la que entrará el eclipse en España, y donde la totalidad tendrá mayor duración: más de 1 minuto y 45 segundos.

José Ángel Docobo, catedrático de Astronomía de la USC y coordinador científico del Observatorio Astronómico Ramón María Aller. ROCÍO CIBES

La conexión entre las pantallas de Lalín y Ribadeo será bidireccional para tener el “doble de posibilidades de verlo bien”, explica Docobo. Porque en Galicia saben que las nubes —que son las peores enemigas para ver un eclipse— “son caprichosas” y no quieren perdérselo. Si las dos opciones fallan porque en los dos sitios está nublado, tienen un plan B, que es retransmitir las imágenes del observatorio astronómico de Javalambre, en Teruel. “Pero, afortunadamente, parece que el pronóstico es muy bueno para el día 12 y así rompemos también con el tópico de que en Galicia sempre chove, ¿no?”, afirma el astrónomo.

Como él, millones de españoles y turistas extranjeros estarán el miércoles pendientes del tiempo para disfrutar del día de las dos noches. La primera se producirá en torno a las 20.30 (la hora exacta depende de la localización) y se verá en una franja que va de Galicia a Baleares y cubrirá buena parte de la mitad norte peninsular. Al ser muy cerca del atardecer, con el Sol muy bajo, para tener buena visibilidad no solo habrá que estar dentro de la franja de totalidad, sino también tener el horizonte despejado hacia el oeste: sin edificios, árboles o montañas que interfieran a la vista.

“Yo le recomendaría a cualquier persona del sur de la Comunidad de Madrid, de Andalucía o de Toledo que se desplace unos días antes a la zona de totalidad”, recomienda Jesús Gallego, catedrático de astrofísica de la Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM), que ha visto cinco eclipses en distintas partes del mundo. “Los cálculos dicen que en Madrid va a ser observable al 99%. Eso no vale. Tiene que ser el 100%”.

Quienes como él han visto el Sol completamente tapado por la Luna coinciden: la experiencia en la totalidad es fascinante y completamente diferente a cualquier otro eclipse. “Es el espectáculo más bonito que nos ofrece la naturaleza. Pone los pelos de punta a todo el mundo”, dice María Ángela del Castillo Alarcos, directora y propietaria de la Escuela de Ciencias-Observatorio Astronómico de Titaguas, en Valencia, que ha visto siete en distintos países: de México a China. “No he visto ninguno en el que la gente no grite. La sensación de hacerse de noche siendo de día y que en escasos minutos o segundos se te vuelva a hacer de día es maravillosa”.

La lotería astronómica le toca a España

Aunque, en promedio, cada 18 meses hay un eclipse de Sol total como este en un lugar de la Tierra, para que se repita en un mismo punto geográfico, tienen que pasar, por lo general, más de 100 años. Por eso, este será especial en España, que además el próximo año recibirá otro eclipse de Sol total en el extremo sur de la Península, y en Ceuta y Melilla. Y en 2028 habrá otro anular, una auténtica lotería astronómica, que se ha llamado el Trío de Eclipses. En el de este 12 de agosto, nuestro país recibirá la totalidad en un 40% de su territorio, y será el único del mundo en poderlo ver junto a algunas zonas de Islandia y un rinconcito de Portugal. Además, sucede en plenas vacaciones de verano, por lo que se espera una enorme afluencia de visitantes.

A los turistas astronómicos que hicieron colgar el cartel de lleno en algunos alojamientos del interior del país con los cielos más limpios para la observación desde hace más de un año, hay que sumar los millones de personas que se desplazarán para ver el eclipse en su totalidad en estos días. Entre las provincias donde más durará están algunas de las más despobladas de España, como León, Palencia, Burgos, Soria y zonas del sur de Aragón.

Para Frank Babinger, profesor de Geografía en la Facultad de Comercio y Turismo de la UCM, la repercusión turística del fenómeno será “máxima” y beneficiará a lugares menos conocidos de España. “La gente que tiene casas, restaurantes y hoteles tiene una oportunidad única para hacer su agosto”, sostiene. El verdadero reto, apunta, será que los visitantes vuelvan después del eclipse, para lo que propone no focalizarse solo en el evento astronómico, sino en lo que hay alrededor, como la naturaleza, el patrimonio o la gastronomía.

Según el informe El Trío Ibérico: una oportunidad para el desarrollo turístico de la España interior, elaborado por la consultora Afi para Airbnb, este eclipse junto con los de los dos próximos años son “una oportunidad excepcional para dinamizar la España interior, con capacidad para atraer más de un millón de viajeros adicionales”. El estudio estima que el de este año puede generar un impacto económico de 421 millones de euros de Valor Añadido Bruto.

La cruz de la moneda es el alza de precios brutal al que se están enfrentando especialmente quienes están buscando un alojamiento a última hora. Según un análisis de más de 5.500 anuncios en Booking publicado esta semana por EL PAÍS, las tarifas se han disparado en la franja de la totalidad: en 90 días, los precios se multiplicaron por seis en Soria, donde una habitación está en torno a unos 900 euros, o por ocho en Zaragoza, donde cuesta en torno a los 500.

Una ‘operación salida’ en lugares inesperados

La organización del eclipse, que está coordinando la Comisión Interministerial del Gobierno Central con las autoridades locales y autonómicas, será un “reto para multitud de organismos”, como ha reconocido la Dirección General de Tráfico, que se está preparando para un acontecimiento “tan único como fugaz” por el volumen de traslados que generará en plena temporada alta.

Un grupo de personas mira el eclipse en Russellville, Arkansas, el 8 de abril de 2024. Jonathan Newton (The Washington Post/Getty Images)

Tráfico estima que el 12 de agosto puede haber hasta 1,5 millones de desplazamientos adicionales hacia las zonas de totalidad. Esa es la media de viajeros diarios en una operación salida de vacaciones. El problema es que no hay datos de hacia dónde irán. Los gobiernos municipales y autonómicos han elegido cientos de puntos de observación con buena visibilidad para tratar de gestionar las multitudes y minimizar movilizaciones, pero en la práctica es imposible saber cuántas personas acudirán a cada uno de ellos y cómo llegarán.

En la mente de las autoridades españolas están los atascos masivos que se produjeron en los eclipses totales de Estados Unidos de 2017 y 2024, unos eventos que también generaron un aumento de accidentes. Por eso, la DGT ha recomendado viajar solo si es necesario y, de hacerlo, planearlo con antelación y en ningún caso aparcar en los arcenes para facilitar el acceso de los equipos de emergencia.

Otro riesgo asociado a las concentraciones como esta son los incendios, que se intensifica en una España especialmente seca y calurosa. Por eso, las comunidades que atraerán a más visitantes han prohibido desde acceder a parques naturales y áreas protegidas con vehículos de motor, a hacer fogatas y han cancelado fiestas y macrofestivales. El ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, pidió el jueves durante la presentación del dispositivo especial de seguridad para el eclipse, que contará con 24.000 guardias civiles desplegados, “responsabilidad y máxima prudencia” a los ciudadanos, y les recordó que disfrutar del evento debe ser “compatible con la protección del medio natural y el cumplimiento estricto de las medidas de prevención”.

¿En qué debemos fijarnos?

Esas medidas de cuidado del entorno de observación las conoce bien Jesús Gallego, el catedrático de astrofísica de la UCM, después de ver cinco eclipses en Venezuela, Europa Central, en la Libia de Gadafi —donde les tocó viajar acompañados por un comisario político—, en Australia y en la Isla de Pascua. Allí, viendo cómo la Luna tapaba el sol en la remota isla de Rapa Nui y entre moáis, escuchó por la radio el gol de Iniesta que convirtió a España en campeona del mundo por primera vez hace 16 años. Como la felicidad de que tu país gane un Mundial o el concierto de un artista favorito, “cuando uno considera que algo es excepcionalmente bonito, pues lo quiere compartir con sus personas queridas”, afirma Gallego. Por eso, este año que él será anfitrión de un grupo de cazaeclipses que vienen de distintos lugares —desde distintas universidades de Estados Unidos a México y Venezuela—, al grupo le acompañarán 15 miembros de su familia.

Todos lo verán en la provincia de Guadalajara. Se alojarán en el Parador Nacional de Molina de Aragón. Su primera opción era el de Sigüenza, pero cuando fue a preguntar hace dos años “ya estaba reservado por un grupo de japoneses desde un año antes”. Saldrán al campo temprano el miércoles para preparar sus equipos y hacer pruebas con los telescopios. Porque mientras todos miramos al Sol, este ofrecerá una oportunidad única para conocer sus secretos. El mayor proyecto científico se hará en Palencia con el proyecto NATE (las siglas en inglés del Telescopio para el Eclipse del Norte de África), que continuará el año que viene en el eclipse de Marruecos para estudiar la desconocida corona solar.

Evolución del eclipse de sol total del 8 de abril de 2024 que se vio en Estados Unidos. Houston Chronicle/Getty Images

¿Y nosotros, en qué deberíamos fijarnos? “Lo que emociona ya no es solo la oscuridad”, dice la divulgadora Del Castillo. Antes, podremos disfrutar de 55 minutos de parcialidad en los que, con las gafas puestas, podremos ir viendo cómo la Luna va tapando al Sol. Cuando el Sol está prácticamente cubierto, “lo primero que asoma pueden ser los relieves de la Luna: las montañas, las vaguadas, los cráteres. Puede que por ahí se escape un poquito de luz. Son las famosas perlas de Baily”, explica. “Finalmente, aparece un destello, el último rayito de sol que puede salir entre alguna vaguada antes de taparse. Entonces, nos podemos quitar las gafas y aparece una corona que puede ser más grande o más pequeña, dependiendo de la actividad que tenga el Sol”.

En ese breve lapso de tiempo de la totalidad, que puede ser de hasta 1 minuto y 40 segundos para los más afortunados, también se podrán ver algunos planetas cercanos. Los expertos recomiendan disfrutar del momento y no perder el tiempo fotografiando al Sol. Si quieres grabar algo, es mejor grabar un video de las reacciones, dicen. El Sol nos permitirá el próximo miércoles, por unos instantes, levantar la vista de nuestros móviles para admirar la grandeza del Universo. Pero además de hacia arriba, el eclipse también será una oportunidad única para que millones de españoles y turistas miren hacia adentro y disfruten de algunos de los lugares más desconocidos de la España interior.

World.title: ¿Qué pasará cuando la Luna tape el Sol? En qué debes fijarte para apreciar el eclipse total
World.content:
La totalidad durará tan solo unos segundos, pero sucederán cosas inusuales tanto en el cielo como a nuestro alrededor. Repasamos qué esperar antes, durante y después del gran fenómeno astronómico

Este miércoles 12 de agosto, por unos segundos y en casi 4.000 municipios de España, se hará de noche en pleno atardecer. Será uno de los mayores espectáculos astronómicos que existen, pero también de los más breves. Tendremos una ventana de apenas dos segundos (desde Derio, Vizcaya) hasta un máximo de 110 (por ejemplo, desde Navia, Asturias) para fijarnos en lo que ocurra en el cielo. Y también en la Tierra.

Estos son algunos de los fenómenos que sucederán antes, durante, y después de la totalidad. Reparar en ellos nos permitirá apreciar y recordar algo que, en la Península, no sucedía desde 1905.

Antes de la totalidad

Los eclipses de sol ocurren cuando la Luna se interpone entre el Sol y la Tierra, y suceden, de media, dos veces al año en todo el globo. Son una coincidencia astronómica: el Sol es 400 veces más grande que la Luna y, a su vez, está 400 veces más lejos que el satélite. Esto hace que, desde la Tierra, la Luna pueda cubrir exactamente todo el disco solar y produzca esta “sombra” sobre nuestro planeta.

La sombra recorrerá la península Ibérica desde el noroeste hasta el sureste. También se observará como parcial en el norte del continente americano, buena parte de Europa y el oeste de África. La sombra de totalidad partirá del océano Ártico, rozará el noreste de Groenlandia y un extremo de Islandia, cruzará el Atlántico y entrará en la península Ibérica, que recorrerá de oeste a este. Para España, será un fenómeno de atardecer, y el eclipse llegará ya en sus últimas fases.

A Coruña será la primera capital de provincia donde será visible: comenzará a las 19:31 y la totalidad ocurrirá a las 20:27, con un minuto y 16 segundos de duración. El último lugar donde será visible será en las Baleares, en la isla de Formentera, donde la totalidad será a las 20:33 y durará 40 segundos; el Sol se pondrá antes de que la última fase del eclipse acabe. Los cascos urbanos de Madrid y Barcelona quedan fuera de la banda. Ahí no habrá totalidad, solo eclipse parcial.

Antes y después de la totalidad se podrán apreciar fenómenos únicos. Uno de ellos es el anillo de diamantes, que ocurre cuando la Luna ya se ha interpuesto casi completamente ante el disco solar y solo quedará ese fragmento final de luz directa en una pequeña zona, que recordará a un anillo que tiene un gran diamante.

Unos segundos después veremos cómo el anillo se fragmenta en pequeñas bolas de luz: se llaman perlas de Baily, y se producen porque la Luna no es una esfera lisa, sino que tiene relieve, como montañas y cráteres, y los últimos rayos del Sol se cuelan por ellos. Además de producir un bonito efecto visual, estas perlas han tenido un importante valor científico para el estudio de la topografía de la Luna, como relata el IGN en su guía para ver el eclipse.

La aparición de la corona solar es uno de los momentos más esperados de un eclipse de este calibre. La corona es la atmósfera del Sol, una capa que rodea la estrella y que es muy difícil de ver en condiciones normales. Curiosamente, la corona solar alcanza temperaturas de millones de grados centígrados, mucho más altas que la superficie del Sol (de unos 5.500 grados). Cuando aparezca la corona, será el único momento de todo el eclipse en que nos podremos quitar las gafas homologadas y contemplarlo sin protección.

“La Luna es, en cierto sentido, el mejor instrumento para observar la corona solar que existe. Durante la totalidad, bloquea el disco solar con una precisión extraordinaria”, explica a EL PAÍS el astrónomo Rafael Bachiller, director del Observatorio Astronómico Nacional y del Real Observatorio de Madrid. “Por eso los eclipses totales siguen siendo científicamente muy valiosos”.

Sin embargo, el eclipse de este 12 de agosto tendrá lugar con el Sol muy bajo sobre el horizonte, por lo que la corona podría no ser tan nítida como en otros eclipses registrados. “La dispersión, la turbulencia y la propia extinción atmosférica pueden reducir el contraste y la definición. Desde la Comisión Científica para el Trío de Eclipses venimos advirtiendo precisamente que para observar el eclipse del 12 de agosto se necesita contar con un horizonte muy despejado hacia el oeste”, advierte Bachiller, por lo que será indispensable consultar los sitios recomendados donde la visibilidad esté garantizada.

La totalidad

Durante la totalidad de un eclipse, la Luna bloquea la luz del Sol y desaparece repentinamente la radiación solar, que es lo que calienta la superficie terrestre. En otras palabras, oscurecerá de golpe. “Durante la totalidad, no solo se oscurece el cielo que tenemos encima, sino que el horizonte adquiere un extraño aspecto crepuscular en todas las direcciones. Es como si estuviéramos en el centro de una puesta de sol gigantesca”, detalla Bachiller.

Esta oscuridad repentina que va a generar el eclipse total solar podría cambiar el comportamiento de los animales, aunque no todos de la misma manera, ni en la misma intensidad. Según Joan Montaner, biólogo del Oceanogràfic de Valencia, “en las aves es donde más se puede observar un cambio de comportamiento”, tal y como expone a EL PAÍS. “Durante un eclipse intentan buscar refugio y se esconden para dormir y se queda todo en silencio. Tras esos dos minutos, empieza otra vez a entrar la luz del Sol y de repente empiezan a hacer el canto de cuando amanece”, señala el biólogo, un comportamiento que “se puede observar, por ejemplo, con las palomas: puede ser que dejen de volar o se posen, buscando refugio. En el monte, puede ser que las aves se metan en las copas de los árboles”.

Una investigación durante el eclipse de 2017 en Estados Unidos detalla que el 75% de las especies observadas durante el evento modificó su comportamiento hacia conductas propias de la noche. “Pero no debemos imaginar que todos los animales van a reaccionar de forma espectacular”, alerta Rafael Bachiller, pues la respuesta “dependerá mucho de la especie y del entorno”.

Un eclipse como el que sucederá el miércoles es una gran oportunidad para seguir investigando dichos cambios. De hecho, varios zoológicos y acuarios de toda España se han aliado para comprobar los efectos de los animales en este y los otros dos eclipses que habrá en España en 2027 y 2028. “En el Oceanogràfic vamos a observar a ocho especies diferentes que vamos a monitorizar”, detalla Montaner.

El eclipse del 12 de agosto es una ocasión única para saber más sobre el comportamiento de los animales, pues un fenómeno así sucede muy pocas veces y en España vamos a poder presenciar tres eclipses en tres años. “Nosotros nunca hemos observado nada igual; puedes leer artículos, hablar con gente que sí lo ha vivido, pero al final no lo hemos vivido”, reconoce el biólogo. “Lo más esperable es la desorientación, porque los animales tampoco han vivido nunca un eclipse. Es un periodo de tiempo muy corto en el que cambia todo por completo”, añade.

Más frío y “viento de eclipse”

En el eclipse de Estados Unidos de 2024 se notaron descensos de entre 2 y 5 grados en la franja de la totalidad. “La temperatura no cae de golpe como si accionásemos un interruptor”, explica Bachiller, y añade que “el cambio de iluminación sí es prácticamente instantáneo, pero la respuesta atmosférica necesita un cierto tiempo”. En Estados Unidos, la máxima bajada de la temperatura o de rachas de viento se registró media hora después de la totalidad.

El descenso de la temperatura puede ocasionar cambios de presión que modifiquen las circulaciones de aire próximas al suelo: es lo que se llama el “viento del eclipse”. En España, “el efecto producido por el eclipse se superpondrá al que normalmente tiene lugar al final del día”, asegura Bachiller, “por eso no esperaría necesariamente un descenso de varios grados como el que se puede observar en determinadas circunstancias durante un eclipse que ocurre con el Sol muy alto sobre el horizonte”.

Durante la totalidad, si por un momento nos fijamos en otros puntos brillantes alrededor del disco, podremos ver Júpiter en la parte inferior derecha del eclipse y, siguiendo la diagonal hacia abajo, Mercurio. Hasta entonces eran poco visibles debido a la luz del día, pero el paso de la Luna por delante del Sol permitirá ver esos dos planetas, si la elevación del terreno nos lo permite.

Cuando termine la totalidad

Si nos hemos quitado las gafas para contemplar la corona solar –recordemos que solo durante la totalidad podemos prescindir de las gafas sin dañarnos la vista–, es el momento de volver a ponérselas para ver cómo la Luna deshace el eclipse hacia el otro lado. La secuencia se reproducirá en sentido inverso: desaparecerá la corona solar, se verán las perlas de Baily y, posteriormente, el anillo de diamantes.

Otro fenómeno al que prestar atención justo después de la totalidad son las bandas de sombra. Son unas franjas muy débiles de luz y oscuridad que se mueven, y que se pueden ver en superficies claras. “En determinadas condiciones pueden observarse sobre superficies claras justo antes y después de la totalidad”, explica Bachiller.

Cómo son las bandas de sombra Lo sentimos, su navegador no soporta la etiqueta de vídeo. Bandas de sombra durante el eclipse total en Dallas, Estados Unidos, en 2024. Fuente: Youtube (@gabrielbn).

Su origen está relacionado con las pequeñas fluctuaciones que produce la atmósfera en la luz procedente del Sol, según detalla la NASA. Las bandas de sombra las produce el mismo efecto que hace que las estrellas titilen cuando las vemos desde la Tierra.

Pocas veces se alinean tantas casualidades astronómicas. Justamente la noche del 12 al 13 de agosto, cuando finalice el eclipse, será el momento máximo de las Perseidas, una “lluvia de estrellas” también conocida como Lágrimas de San Lorenzo. Este 2026, la mejor hora será entre las 4 y las 6 de la madrugada, “aunque se considera que la actividad puede ser intensa entre las 23.00 horas del día 12 y las 11.00 de la mañana del 13”, según el IGN.

Las Perseidas son partículas que chocan con nuestra atmósfera. En concreto, son como granos de arena que han sido liberados por el cometa 109P/Swift-Tuttle a lo largo de los años y que se encuentran en su órbita. Cada año, a principios de agosto, nuestro planeta cruza la órbita de este cometa y estas partículas entran en contacto con la atmósfera de la Tierra a gran velocidad. La fricción las calienta y las vaporiza.

Además del eclipse de este 12 de agosto, en España tendremos dos más en los próximos dos años, algo muy inusual. En el eclipse total del 2 de agosto de 2027, la totalidad cubrirá Ceuta y Melilla, casi toda la provincia de Cádiz y Málaga y el sur de las provincias de Granada y Almería. El 26 de enero de 2028, otro eclipse, esta vez anular –la Luna no cubre totalmente el disco solar–, se verá desde varias comunidades autónomas del sureste peninsular. Este completará la tríada de eclipses ibéricos de 2026-2028. No será posible observar otro eclipse solar total desde España hasta 2053.

Después de esa tríada histórica, España tendrá que esperar hasta 2053 para volver a vivir un eclipse total de Sol. En ciertos años es posible que haya hasta cinco, como ocurrió por última vez en 1935 y no volverá a ocurrir hasta 2206. “Yo voy a verlo desde el Observatorio de Yebes, en Guadalajara”, confiesa Rafael Bachiller. “Llegado el momento, intentaré hacer algo muy sencillo: dejar durante unos instantes la parte científica a un lado, olvidarme del móvil y de todas las pantallas e instrumentos, y disfrutar del espectáculo”, reconoce el astrónomo. “Será un auténtico privilegio poder levantar la mirada y contemplar finalmente esos minutos de totalidad”.

World.title: Ajax, ING and Ace & Tate hit by data breach
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Football club Ajax, bank ING and eyewear chain Ace & Tate have been caught up in the data breach at logistics firm CEVA Logistics, which came to light this week when Bol and De Bijenkorf warned customers their details may have been exposed.

CEVA handles deliveries for the companies and had access to the customer data needed to fulfil orders. The firm says it cannot rule out that personal details were leaked, although the companies affected say no payment details, usernames or passwords were taken.

Whether addresses, email addresses or phone numbers were exposed remains unclear.

At ING, the breach affects customers who ordered physical products through the bank’s rewards points scheme.

Ajax has advised supporters to be extra alert to phishing messages in the coming weeks. The club and Ace & Tate have both reported the breach to privacy watchdog AP, as Bol did earlier this week.

Ace & Tate has warned customers that current orders may be delayed, although online ordering is still running. CEVA said it would respond to the breach at a later stage.

World.title: Actor Peter Faber, star of Dutch cinema’s golden age, dies at 82
World.content:
Peter Faber, one of the best-known faces of Dutch film and theatre for half a century, has died at the age of 82.

Faber was admitted to hospital in early July with breathing difficulties related to untreatable heart problems, his family told news agency ANP.

He broke through in the 1970s, widely regarded as the golden age of Dutch cinema, with roles in Keetje Tippel and Paul Verhoeven’s wartime classic Soldaat van Oranje – the film that later spawned the long-running musical which closed last month after 16 years.

He also took the title role in the 1976 film of Max Havelaar, Multatuli’s classic novel about Dutch colonial rule, and appeared alongside Sean Connery and Anthony Hopkins in Richard Attenborough’s A Bridge Too Far.

Faber began his career as a co-founder of Het Werkteater, an Amsterdam collective set up in the early 1970s to shake up Dutch theatre with performances about ordinary people and recognisable emotions. He won the Louis d’Or, the top Dutch theatre prize for a male actor, twice.

He kept working into his eighties. His final film role came in 2023 in Sweet Dreams, the Dutch entry for the 2024 Oscars, in which he appeared alongside his son Jesse.

Faber often spoke about his difficult upbringing, part of which he spent living on the streets of Amsterdam as a teenager. In 2008 he set up the Peter Faber Foundation to help young people build confidence, and to “make the switch from destructive to creative energy”. Its motto is “I can do it, I want it, I’m doing it. Now!”

A public memorial service will be held at Het Zonnehuis in Amsterdam-Noord on Monday between 10am and midday.

World.title: Cabinet rules out compensation for drought-hit businesses
World.content:
Despite the country’s continuing water shortage, entrepreneurs feeling the squeeze won’t be receiving any help from the government any time soon.

“There are arrangements in place for the event of a natural disaster, such as the flooding in Limburg in 2021, but we are not there yet,” infrastructure and water management minister Vincent Karremans said while visiting Nijmegen on Thursday.

“We don’t have the money in the account either. We can’t help it that it isn’t raining.”

Maarten Ouboter, a technician for the Amstel, Gooi and Vecht water authority, told DutchNews: “The question is: how much is a government – the public – responsible for the weather? The minister was clear: droughts can happen.”

Low water levels are hurting everyone from inland vessels that can’t sail down dwindling rivers to houseboat owners on the Rhine who have effectively been marooned. Several locks have been closed, ferries have been cancelled and the economically important Twente Canal, reported broadcaster NOS, is also inaccessible.

And while Karremans estimates that the economic damage to businesses runs “into the tens, if not hundreds of millions of euros”, he views the water shortage as an “entrepreneurial risk, after all” – not a natural disaster.

A shortage but not a crisis

For now, the country’s water level remains at 2 – a shortage but not yet a crisis. That could change if the drought continues for another few weeks. But the government maintains its priorities are preserving the country’s dikes and ensuring enough available drinking water, not propping up businesses.

“We are now at a point that the rivers flowing into our low-lying delta have never been so low in August,” said Ouboter, who focuses on the Amsterdam area. “We are comparable to 1947, but that was in November.”

Using a football analogy, he said the drought “in June was ‘second league’; in July it was ‘first league’; in August, it’s Champions League.”

Boosting water storage

Karremans said more water must be stored for the future, including in places like the IJsselmeer and the Volkerak-Zoommeer. The cabinet is currently working on the Freshwater Delta Plan to ensure rainwater captured in the spring, for example, can be used in drier months.

In Amsterdam, an innovative system of wadis – dry water ditches – catches rainwater that can be distributed later where needed and also absorbs extra rainwater to prevent flooding.

“The way we think about water has changed,” said Ton Hilhorst, the chief garden designer at Amsterdam’s Artis zoo. “Water was always seen as the enemy, but now we must keep it in the country, not pump it out.”

Weather forecasters are predicting another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with rain unlikely in the current week.

World.title: Philip Morris rebuked over AI campaign against EU tobacco rules
World.content:
The Dutch advertising standards watchdog RCC has reprimanded tobacco behemoth Philip Morris for an AI-powered ad campaign that it says violated the country’s tobacco advertising ban.

As the EU prepares its biggest tobacco tightening rules in 15 years, the public was invited to share its views via comments.

But a recent investigation by broadcaster NOS and the journalism platform Pointer found that Philip Morris used AI to generate hundreds of fake “citizen” responses opposing tougher EU rules on vapes, which along with other cigarette alternatives like e-cigarettes and heated tobacco, now account for 40% of the company’s revenue.

Here’s how the campaign worked: Philip Morris put up yellow posters carrying QR codes in tobacco shops under the slogan “Your Voice Your Choice.” Scanning the code led to a tool that asked multiple-choice questions and then an option to write a first-person text, which users could then send to the Commission.

The investigation found that some 71% of responses from the Netherlands were written by AI, the second highest after Portugal.

The RCC had several problems with the campaign, including that the text generator was paid for and owned by Philip Morris. The company defended its actions by saying it contributed to the public debate.

“The fact that the statements are framed as a call for public consultation does not detract from their commercial character,” said the watchdog.

The written responses also portray alternative tobacco products positively, which the RCC says constitutes advertising and therefore violates the tobacco advertising ban.

Doctors

In June, a group of doctors and healthcare campaign groups made a formal complaint to the RCC, saying the “misleading” campaign used an AI tool to influence European decision-making on tobacco and nicotine products.

Lawyer Laura van Gijn, who represents the doctors, told NOS that violating the tobacco advertising ban is a criminal offence. “This decision is a clear signal to the tobacco industry that digital influence campaigns do not fall outside the scope of the advertising ban, even when packaged as citizen participation. This precedent is relevant for similar campaigns elsewhere in Europe.”

World.title: No more “shame lips”: Dutch dictionary adds new word for labia
World.content:
Women’s rights groups are applauding the latest addition to the definitive Dutch dictionary Dikke Van Dale of the word labia: vulvalippen, added alongside the word schaamlippen.

While both words mean labia, the old schaamlippen translates as “shame lips”, which the organisations say is stigmatising as compared to the more neutral “vulva lips”.

“We should just mention these parts in our education with children and young people,” artist Esther van der Valk told broadcaster NOS. “People now know that this is a normal word, and with that we can break the taboo.”

Van der Valk is a member of Dolle Mina, the women’s rights group that was founded in the Netherlands in 1969 and has been advocating for the inclusion of vulvalippen in the Dutch dictionary to counter stigmatisation. They’re joined by Schaamteloos, a more recent campaign seeking to change language and attitudes regarding female anatomy.

Body positive

While schaamlippen will remain in the dictionary, the addition of vulvalippen means the word gets official Dutch language status – proof, say the activists, that the normalisation of sexuality via language can be achieved if enough people want it.

Schaamlippen is not the only word where shame is embedded in its name. There’s schaamhaar – “shame hair” – which is the name for pubic hair, schaambeen (shame bone) for pubic bone and even schaamstreek (shame area) for pubic area.

But Schaamteloos says it had to start somewhere, so it picked schaamlippen. “Everyone has pubic hair, a pubic bone, and a pubic area,” says the group, but “only half of us have labia – or ‘shame lips’ … which adds to a disproportionately large amount of trouble due to the taboo on talking about this.”

While some doctors and even the media have taken to using vulvalippen, it’s not yet part of the everyday Dutch vernacular.

That may change when the new anatomically correct word is included in the Dikke van Dale. That’s expected to happen during its next online update, likely this Autumn.

World.title: Four arrested for death threat against Breda mayor
World.content:
Police have arrested four men suspected of threatening to kill Breda mayor Paul Depla, after a photograph found on a football supporter’s phone revealed new evidence for a case that had stalled.

A banner bearing the words “Depla Dood” (Depla dead) was hung on the front of a café in the city’s Meidoornstraat on March 8, when NAC Breda played Feyenoord. Depla reported the threat to the police, but in May prosecutors said the case had halted because the suspects could not be linked to the banner.

A breakthrough came when several NAC supporters were arrested over rioting around the club’s match against Heerenveen on May 10 and their phones were seized, police said. On one of them, officers found a photograph of the banner in which four men could be identified.

The four – three from Breda, aged 16, 32 and 34, and a 24-year-old from Oosterhout – were arrested on Thursday and will be questioned. Threatening a public official carries a maximum prison sentence of four years.

It is unclear what prompted the threat, but broadcaster NOS reported it may have followed a warning from the city council to a different café, which had planned to host a pre-match party for the club’s hardcore supporters.

When the owners called the party off, the group gathered at the Meidoornstraat café instead, where the banner was hung.

Threats and intimidation against Dutch public officials are a growing concern. Some 45% of local and regional political office holders, including mayors, told a 2024 home affairs ministry survey they had faced aggression in the preceding year.

World.title: Warm, dry weekend ahead as drought shows no sign of ending
World.content:
The Netherlands is set for another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with barely a drop of rain likely for the coming week, according to forecasters.

Friday will be calm and dry with temperatures of 21 to 25°, with morning cloud in the north east giving way to sunshine. Saturday will be sunny and slightly warmer, at 25 to 28°, before temperatures climb to around 30° inland on Sunday.

A brief cooler spell will push maximums down to around 25° on Tuesday, but forecasters expect the warmth to return later in the week – without any significant rain.

The dry spell means no let-up for the ongoing drought, which has pushed the Rhine to record low levels and prompted water use restrictions in several regions.

World.title: Childcare benefits falling short for most parents: CBS
World.content:
Almost two-thirds of parents who claim childcare benefits pay more than the government’s maximum hourly rate, leaving them with hundreds of euros in costs the benefit does not cover, according to national statistics agency CBS.

Parents claiming the benefit spent an average of €10,510 on childcare in 2025, of which 68% was covered, up from 65% in 2024. The benefit was raised in both years as a step towards the government plan for near-free childcare.

But childcare providers are free to set their own fees, and the benefit only applies to costs up to a ceiling fixed by the government each year. In 2025, 63% of parents paid more than the maximum rate for at least one child.

On average, parents paid €3,340 towards childcare themselves last year – €2,860 in regular contributions, plus an extra €480 to cover fees above the official maximum.

The share of parents paying over the ceiling varies widely. In Nunspeet, Bloemendaal, Houten and Midden-Delfland, almost 90% pay more than the maximum rate, compared with just 8% on the island of Ameland. The proportion is highest in the provinces of Utrecht and Noord-Holland and lowest in Friesland and Groningen.

Households in the lowest income group paid an average of €1,190 towards childcare, or 11% of the total cost, while the highest earners paid €5,950, just over half the bill.

In total, 719,000 parents claimed the benefit last year for nearly 1.1 million children. More children attended nurseries and after-school clubs, while the number looked after by registered childminders (gastouders) fell by 10,000 to around 95,000.

The cabinet plans to make childcare almost free for working parents from 2029, covering 96% of costs regardless of income – a scheme that has been repeatedly delayed.

World.title: Remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during World War Two have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools (as pictured above). The announcement comes amid ongoing tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the so-called Volhynia massacres, sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was responsible for leading the killings of around 100,000 Poles. However, both sides have expressed hope that continued exhumations of victims – most of which are believed to still remain buried in unmarked mass graves in Ukraine – can ease that path towards reconciliation. 📣 Zakończenie tegorocznych prac ekshumacyjnych ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej ❗ Od 13 lipca do 7 sierpnia br. pracownicy Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej, przedsiębiorstwa „Wołyńskie Starożytności” oraz specjalista z zakresu medycyny sądowej z… pic.twitter.com/iDJR5NmdEn — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 7, 2026 The new findings were made in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka, two neighbouring former villages, now depopulated, that were previously part of Poland but, after postwar border changes, are now located in western Ukraine. There, on 30 August 1943, the UPA massacred over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Similar massacres took place in many other villages, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation by the UPA to remove Poles and other minorities from what they saw as Ukrainian territory. Exhumations previously took place in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantlement of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has now announced the result of that work. They have uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit, notes the IPN Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Around 300 personal items, including rosaries, crosses and clothing, were also found during the recent excavations in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. On 30 August, the 83rd anniversary of the massacre, the newly found remains will be buried in a funeral ceremony at the cemetery in Ostrówki. The IPN believes that over 300 further victims still remain buried at unknown locations in the two former villages. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. There have since been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice.
